questions.question: How do sessions and cookies work in Rails?
questions.title: Rails Sessions and Cookies
questions.direct_answer: A session lets you remember a user across requests (who's logged in, what's in their cart) without re-sending data each time. Rails stores a session as a cookie by default (a small key-value store signed and encrypted with credentials) — you write to session[:user_id] = user.id and read session[:user_id]. A cookie is a key-value pair the browser sends with every request to your domain; you set one with cookies[:prefs] = { value: 'dark', expires: 1.year }. Sessions are for auth/state that shouldn't be tampered with; plain cookies are for client-side prefs like a theme.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Storing sensitive data in a plain cookie (not encrypted), or confusing the session cookie with plain cookies.

sections.title: Remembering Users Across Requests
sections.content: A session lets you remember a user across requests — who's logged in, what's in their cart — without re-sending data each time. Rails stores the session as a cookie by default: a small key-value store signed and encrypted with your credentials, so the user can read but not tamper with it. You write session[:user_id] = user.id and read session[:user_id]. A cookie is a key-value pair the browser sends with every request to your domain; you set one with cookies[:prefs] = { value: 'dark', expires: 1.year }. Sessions are for auth and state that shouldn't be tampered with; plain cookies are for client-side preferences like a theme that the client can read and change.

sections.title: Session vs Cookie
sections.content:
The session is stored in a signed/encrypted cookie; plain cookies are client-controlled.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  L[login] --> S[session\[:user_id\] = user.id]
  S --> C[signed+encrypted cookie in browser]
  N[next request] --> C --> R[session\[:user_id\] readable; tamper-evident]
```

sections.title: Sessions and cookies
sections.content:
```ruby
# SESSION (signed + encrypted cookie by default in Rails)
class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    user = User.authenticate(params[:email], params[:password])
    if user
      session[:user_id] = user.id          # remember who's logged in
      redirect_to root_path
    else
      flash[:alert] = 'Invalid credentials'
      render :new
    end  end

  def destroy
    session.delete(:user_id)             # log out
    redirect_to root_path
  end
end

# current_user reads the session
def current_user
  @current_user ||= User.find_by(id: session[:user_id]) if session[:user_id]
end

# PLAIN COOKIE (client-side, set with options)
cookies[:theme] = { value: 'dark', expires: 1.year }   # client can read/change
t = cookies[:theme]                                    # 'dark'
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Storing sensitive data in a plain cookie (not encrypted) — use the session.
Confusing the session cookie with plain cookies — the session is signed/encrypted.
Forgetting to delete the session on logout (the user stays 'logged in').

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A session remembers a user across requests; Rails stores it as a signed+encrypted cookie.
session[:user_id]= to write; session[:user_id] to read; session.delete on logout.
A plain cookie (cookies[:k]=) is client-controlled — use it for prefs, not auth.
Sessions are tamper-evident (encrypted); plain cookies the client can read and change.
current_user typically reads session[:user_id] to find the logged-in user.
